chapterTitle: Chapter 3: Synaptic Memoriam of a steel fossil shell
editorText:
<$Proj_H::2>Checking the Saddle. <!$Proj_H::2>

The ship itself was much smaller than its holding bay, out of place. The scaled of the bay suggested it had been designed for something much, much larger. The sheer enormity of the structure detracted from the little ship's aesthetic and design; it felt insignificant in comparison. John walked slowly up to the underbelly of the vessel, prying closely at its hull, observing the alien insignia etched into its side. A blanket of dust obscured its view from the others, as John, in direct line of sight, his inbuilt computer began trying to translate although struggled, splurting out only fragments at a time. Curiosity gripped him as he raised his palm to its belly. He seemed to approach the ship with caution like it was alive, more than just a shell of cold steel enshrouding technology buried deep within the mountain but an exoskeleton protecting organs its creators had so delicately pieced together.

As confidence rose within him, he pressed his palm flat on its underbelly then wiped away the dust that once obscured the insignia in two smooth firm sweeps. John's kitten had compared encrypted data banks from files buried deep in the lost facilities archives translating the strange language. John skipped a breath in thought for a moment, taken aback by the now revealed name, then chuckled, "Well, that's a little weird!"

Tau was silently captivated, trying to piece together in her mind how the thrusters' careful placement around the ship would fly her. Vector lines formed around its shell outward in her mind like pen to pad. "Huh," said Tau. "Did you say something, Cap?"

"The name of the ship, at least that's what I think it is... it's the same as my childhood horse on the farm I grew up on."

Tau wandered over to John's side, looking up at the insignia with him. "I can't make it out... B... beve..." Tau lipped at the insignia like a confused child.

"Here," said John, flicking her the lost facilities files from his wrist terminal. "See if that helps." Slowly her HUD began to translate the insignia, the word slowly came out of her lips as each letter turned over. "Beverly..." its edges kissed by the dusty blanket of time. "Beautiful name, though strange for curation from something made in a lab," Tau concluded.

"It makes you wonder how pure sentients' personalities are formed, from what memories? What made them who they are to begin with, do they have set precursors with selected memories added on top, or just pure akin programming from the start?"

Shai was scanning over the medical equipment and rations in the trip supply brought over by Tebo. "Would you happen to have an inventory file, my metal friend?" said Shai.

"Sure, lassy." Tebo's mechanical legs sprang with a joyous formality at her request.

"I've just sent you over the inventory data," said John. Tebo had linked with a mere thought, the file paths to their scheduled supply inventory. He wandered over to Shai leaning in softly like a warm smile, his hands on his hips.

"You're all in for a long flight ahead. Once you make it past the orbital blockade, you humies will need all the nutrients you can get while you sleep through your high-g burn." A supply crate hovered no more than half an inch above metal tracks that had been recessed into the slab of the ship's bay, one leading to each of the bays that stretched on for about three football fields.

The supply crate opened out, presenting several compartments, one with medical supplies, another loaded with a variety of fruits, meat, poultry, as well as canisters loaded with nutrient-rich liquids that, premade, looked as though they had been designed like cartridges. Each labeled with the strange insignia that could be seen throughout the sentient hold.

"I'm beginning to like these guys," muffled Tex, as he helped himself to an apple from the produce compartment with yet another crisp chomp. "Damn... these are good!" he proceeded, chewing through it like a wild malnourished horse that had just survived the winter.

"First the ship name, now horse chops over, I am really getting taken back to the paddock," said John.

"Maybe it's a sign you should get back in that saddle, cowboy," said Tau, resting her hand gently on John's shoulder with a slight eased shake. She looked on through the rear cargo hold of Beverly to the bridge. She nodded her head at the silhouette of something John felt all too familiar with, letting out a soft smile like she knew deep down, John would be in a state of nostalgia if he just lingered a little while further inside. The hangar light dimly illuminated the outline of a black object, reaching farther down into the cargo hold of the ship to catch John’s eye. The pilot’s seat of the Beverly was constructed of a pristine black leather. It sat there silently, alluring, untouched evident by the specs of dust that gently lined it’s contours. John looked confused for a moment, then slowly made his way up through the beverly’s belly to the guided like a firefly toward the seat. John rested his hand on the shoulder hilt of the chair, running it down it’s side, as though caressing with his palm. It seemed like it had filled a void in his heart he had forgotten about.

“This doesn’t look like a ship built by the sentient” His voice was riddled with question as he became lost in the relic from the past, that laid now quietly in a womb of technological feat beyond it’s original birthplace. He felt himself being drawn deeper to it, comforted by it’s hold. It felt familiar, although he had never flown such a ship, at least he thought that he hadn’t as far back as he could remember.

The outside of the Beverley was all but smooth, with fine contours like a stealth bird. Defences weren't entirely apparent, which was a little concerning for a team about to slip through an orbital defense barrage. Yet the inside of the Beverley was nostalgic for John, as if he had seen it before in some distant dream.

The cockpit of the Beverley was small—so small it humbled you, especially for a squad of Protectants who had just come from living aboard a ship like the Balaenoptera with its spacious hallways and open-design bridge.

"Why does this feel like something from Back to the Future?" Shai had just eased her head into the cockpit from the cargo hold. "Don't press the red button." Tam smiled back at Shai, looking over her shoulder. She had already removed one of the panels under the cockpit dash and was mapping out her control system.

"All good on inventory," said John. "All good, Cap!" Shai shot back. "Good work." John slapped Shai on the shoulder with a friendly squeeze, then made his way back out to where Tex was still stuffing his face, familiarising himself with the point defense cannons along the Beverley's belly.

"How is our firing arc PDCs?" asked John. "Any blind spots?". Tex was crouched over, actuating a switch under the main control panel. "Manual checks showing full range of motion on the gyros," he said, wiping some grease from his forehead and sweating profusely. "The stern port side PDC Y-axis has a limitation at 170°, slight kink, but we can make up for it with the bow port cannon. We are high-tailing it anyway. Unless you plan on paying Marcellus some return love from his theatrics yesterday, we should be fine."

Tex was looking John in the eye with a serious fixture. His eyes screamed vengeance, like he had taken a king hit to the back of the head, and Marcellus was behind it.

“Good work Tex” Said John, dismissing his last comment as a suicide run and shear action on impulse. “High tailing it… I get it” Sighed Tex. Ducking his head back under the PCD’s control panel. “Send me the updated defence sector coverage when you are done!” Said John, making his way over to the loading bay where Tebo was tinkering away. Tebo’s hand was nothing like a hand a usual human hand, despite the obvious design of the sentient to sync with the human neural network. A small probe retracted back forearm, the final component tucked neatly into his index finger seamlessly .John looked at this with amazement and slight concern, then yelled back to Tex still berried deep underneath panels along the internal hull of the ship. “I need to know which soft spots we have so I can turn them away from any heat we might have coming our way!”

Tex didn’t respond initially but he heard the captain nonetheless. His focus acutely honed in on bringing the mid ship’s PDC into an acceptable motion range. “Cap these aren’t the original fittings of the ship.. They’re updates. I don’t think this thing was intended as a gun ship. It’s just not fitted with enough guts to support your typical PDC, I mean unless your firing snow peas at the enemy I don’t know what they were expecting mounting these here”.

Tebo walked over next to John, “Precisely, we didn’t need to reinforce her. The PDC’s we designed are purely for defence purposes. They aren’t meant to breach the armour of typical fleet’s… just ordinance”.. John was silent contemplating what they were getting themselves into. Tex paused his inspection abruptly pulling himself out from under the gunnel where the PDC panels laid. “You mean to tell me we are supposed to intimidate anyone coming at us head on with harsh language!” chuckled Tex. “Aaah heck well I’m your guy, just make sure you have a secure channel to their bridge on max volume before we enter the fight, and I’ll make sure they’re ears are ringing with sweet melodies” Tex stood eyeing off the vague visor of tebo, the usual scattered chatter accross his dome showed a lack of thought. He couldn’t tell if he was being serious or joking.

“If all else fails my friend we do have other measures” Tebo exclaimed. “Lets hope we don’t have to use them. The aim is to slip past the hole without waking the fox”. John paused for a moment looking back to the little android man, “Right Tebo..” Said John, “Theoretically yes”. said Tebo with no emotionin his response. The lack there of strangely instilled John with a silent confidence in his plan. Afterall, they had survived undetected over half a century. He couldn’t fault his logic, whatever it was. He trusted him.
